claim: The somatosensory input that gives rise to the perceptions of pain, itch, cold and heat are initially integrated in the superficial dorsal horn of the spinal cord.
source: The somatosensory input that gives rise to the perceptions of pain, itch, cold and heat are initially integrated in the superficial dorsal horn of the spinal cord.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the anatomical location of somatosensory integration.

claim: The semi-intact somatosensory preparation enables recording from spinal output neurons, while precisely controlling somatosensory input, and simultaneously manipulating specific populations of spinal interneurons.
source: This semi-intact somatosensory preparation enables recording from spinal output neurons, while precisely controlling somatosensory input, and simultaneously manipulating specific populations of spinal interneurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding describing the capabilities of the new preparation developed in this study.

claim: Spinal interneurons show distinct temporal and spatial tuning properties.
source: Our findings suggest that spinal interneurons show distinct temporal and spatial tuning properties.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing different temporal responses and spatial receptive field properties.

claim: Modality selectivity — mechanical, heat and cold — can be assessed in both retrogradely labeled spinoparabrachial projection neurons and genetically labeled spinal interneurons.
source: We also show that modality selectivity — mechanical, heat and cold — can be assessed in both retrogradely labeled spinoparabrachial projection neurons and genetically labeled spinal interneurons.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data showing responses to different stimulus modalities in both cell types.

claim: Interneuron connectivity can be determined via optogenetic activation of specific interneuron subtypes.
source: Finally, we demonstrate that interneuron connectivity can be determined via optogenetic activation of specific interneuron subtypes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data using optogenetic stimulation to map connections between interneurons.

claim: Noxious chemical, mechanical and thermal stimuli are conveyed to the dorsal horn of the spinal cord where they are integrated by excitatory and inhibitory interneurons.
source: Noxious chemical, mechanical and thermal stimuli are conveyed to the dorsal horn of the spinal cord where they are integrated by excitatory and inhibitory interneurons.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about spinal cord function.

claim: Under some circumstances, spinal neural circuits reduce the degree to which noxious input is conveyed to the brain.
source: Under some circumstances, these neural circuits reduce the degree to which noxious input is conveyed to the brain (Gebhart, 2004; Moayedi and Davis, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In some circumstances, somatosensory input is amplified by spinal circuits, leading to allodynia and hyperalgesia, two hallmarks of chronic pain.
source: In others, the somatosensory input is amplified by spinal circuits, leading to allodynia and hyperalgesia, two hallmarks of chronic pain (Sandkühler, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Electrophysiological recording from spinal neurons is one of the best approaches to study the functional connectivity among spinal neurons in detail.
source: Electrophysiological recording from spinal neurons is one of the best approaches to study the functional connectivity among spinal neurons in detail.
evidence: This is based on established scientific knowledge and practice in the field.

claim: Historically, electrophysiological studies of spinal neurons were performed using in vivo recordings.
source: Historically, such studies were performed using in vivo recordings (Brown et al., 1987; Carstens, 1997; Craig et al., 2001; Dickenson and Sullivan, 1986; Jinks and Carstens, 2000, 1999; Koerber et al., 1991; Randic et al., 1988; Torsney and Fitzgerald, 2002; Urch and Dickenson, 2003; Zhang et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: A considerable limitation to in vivo recording approaches is that it is difficult to target known cell types in the dorsal horn.
source: However, a considerable limitation to this approach is that it is difficult to target known cell types in the dorsal horn.
evidence: This is based on inference from the technical limitations of in vivo recording methods.

claim: With the advent of molecular genetic tools, it has been possible to overcome the constraint of targeting known cell types by recording from genetically defined subsets of neurons.
source: With the advent of a new generation of molecular genetic tools, it has been possible to overcome this constraint by recording from genetically defined subsets of neurons (Bourane et al., 2015a, 2015b; Cui et al., 2016; Duan et al., 2014; Hantman et al., 2004; Heinke et al., 2004; Kardon et al., 2014; Peirs et al., 2015; Petitjean et al., 2015; Zeilhofer et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Experiments using molecular genetic tools to target neurons have generally been performed within the context of a spinal slice.
source: Generally, though, these experiments have been performed within the context of a spinal slice, which suffers from the shortcoming that key components of the nociceptive circuit, such as the input, are severed.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of common experimental approaches in the field.

claim: Spinal slice preparations suffer from the shortcoming that key components of the nociceptive circuit, such as the input, are severed.
source: Generally, though, these experiments have been performed within the context of a spinal slice, which suffers from the shortcoming that key components of the nociceptive circuit, such as the input, are severed.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of the limitations of slice preparations.

claim: In spinal slice preparations, spinal circuits are evaluated using electrical stimulation of the whole dorsal roots, which is not physiological.
source: In this context, spinal circuits are evaluated using electrical stimulation of the whole dorsal roots, even though such a stimulus is not physiological.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of common experimental practices and their limitations.

claim: The semi-intact preparation comprises a large portion of spinal cord (~C2 – S3), together with lumbar 2 (L2) and L3 roots, ganglia, saphenous nerve and hindlimb skin (including hindpaw), dissected in continuum.
source: This preparation comprises of a large portion of spinal cord (~C2 – S3), together with lumbar 2 (L2) and L3 roots, ganglia, saphenous nerve and hindlimb skin (including hindpaw), dissected in continuum (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental preparation, supported by data in the form of figures.

claim: Spinal segments L2 and L3 are regions of the spinal cord that are well-suited for visually-guided whole cell recordings because they contain regions of grey matter that are clearly visible between gaps in the roots.
source: Spinal segments L2 and L3, which are targeted by the saphenous nerve, are regions of the spinal cord that are well-suited for visually-guided whole cell recordings because they contain regions of grey matter that are clearly visible between gaps in the roots (Figure 1C, dotted ovals).
evidence: This is based on anatomical observations and experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: The lateral aspect of the dorsal horn is favorable for recordings because the white matter in this region is very thin.
source: In particular, the lateral aspect of the dorsal horn is favorable because the white matter in this region is very thin (Figure 1D, green shaded area).
evidence: This is based on anatomical observations shown in the figure.

claim: Side illumination with a high-powered infrared light emitting diode allowed visualization and patch-clamp recording of cells up to 50 µm from the surface of the spinal cord.
source: To this end, we employed side illumination with a high-powered infrared light emitting diode, which allowed visualization and patch-clamp recording of cells up to 50 µm from the surface of the spinal cord (Figure 1F), consistent with previous reports (Safronov et al., 2007; Szucs et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to previous literature.

claim: At the reversal potential for chloride (VH = −70 mV) only EPSCs are observed.
source: To facilitate the study of both excitatory post-synaptic currents (EPSCs) and inhibitory post-synaptic currents (IPSCs) in the same cells, we took advantage of the fact that at the reversal potential for chloride (VH = −70 mV) only EPSCs are observed, whereas at a depolarized holding potential (VH = −40 mV) it is possible to clearly resolve IPSCs as outward current (Yoshimura and Nishi, 1993).
evidence: This is based on established electrophysiological principles and cited literature.

claim: At a depolarized holding potential (VH = −40 mV) it is possible to clearly resolve IPSCs as outward current.
source: To facilitate the study of both excitatory post-synaptic currents (EPSCs) and inhibitory post-synaptic currents (IPSCs) in the same cells, we took advantage of the fact that at the reversal potential for chloride (VH = −70 mV) only EPSCs are observed, whereas at a depolarized holding potential (VH = −40 mV) it is possible to clearly resolve IPSCs as outward current (Yoshimura and Nishi, 1993).
evidence: This is based on established electrophysiological principles and cited literature.

claim: Approximately half of lamina I neurons showed synaptic currents upon brushing of the anterior hindlimb skin.
source: We found that approximately half of lamina I neurons showed synaptic currents upon brushing of the anterior hindlimb skin.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from recordings.

claim: Brush-evoked EPSCs and IPSCs were observed in one quarter of responding lamina I neurons.
source: Of these, brush-evoked EPSCS and IPSCS (Figure 2A and D) were observed in one quarter of responding lamina I neurons.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: Only EPSCs were observed upon brush stimulation for approximately half of lamina I neurons.
source: In contrast, only EPSCs were observed upon brush stimulation for approximately half of lamina I neurons (Figure 2B and D), whereas only IPSCs were observed in the remaining quarter (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: Only IPSCs were observed upon brush stimulation in the remaining quarter of responding lamina I neurons.
source: In contrast, only EPSCs were observed upon brush stimulation for approximately half of lamina I neurons (Figure 2B and D), whereas only IPSCs were observed in the remaining quarter (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: Of lamina I neurons that receive both excitatory and inhibitory inputs upon stimulation of the skin, the majority (5 of 6) show center-surround receptive fields.
source: Of lamina I neurons that receive both excitatory and inhibitory inputs upon stimulation of the skin, the majority (5 of 6) show this type of center-surround receptive field (Figure 2F), consistent with previous intracellular recordings in cat (Brown et al., 1987; Koerber et al., 2006; Koerber and Mirnics, 1996).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in the figure and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Most lamina I neurons (48 of 61) showed EPSCs only during the period of mechanical stimulation.
source: Most lamina I neurons (48 of 61) showed EPSCs only during the period of mechanical stimulation (Figure 2G and I).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: Approximately one-fifth of lamina I neurons showed a prolonged afterdischarge of EPSCs and action potentials that outlasted the stimulus duration by several seconds.
source: However, approximately one-fifth showed a very distinct temporal response in which a prolonged afterdischarge of EPSCs and action potentials outlasted the stimulus duration by several seconds (Figure 2H and I), consistent with previous findings from recordings in vivo (Woolf and Fitzgerald, 1983).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in the figure and supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Most anterolateral tract projection neurons send their axons to the lateral parabrachial nucleus in the brainstem.
source: Previous work in rat has revealed that most anterolateral tract projection neurons send their axons to the lateral parabrachial nucleus in the brainstem (Al-Khater and Todd, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Half of spinoparabrachial projection neurons were polymodal, responding to both mechanical and thermal stimulation.
source: Half of these neurons were considered to be polymodal because action potentials were evoked in response to both mechanical and thermal stimulation (Figure 3B, C and F).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: Half of spinoparabrachial projection neurons appeared tuned to thermal stimuli, responding to either cold only or cold and heat.
source: The other half appeared tuned to thermal stimuli, responding to either cold only (Figure 3D) or cold and heat (Figure 3E) as summarized (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: Mouse spinal projection neurons in lamina I show modality-selective tuning, like those in cat, rat and monkey.
source: Thus, our data show that the somatosensory preparation can be used to determine stimulus-response properties, and reveal for the first time that mouse spinal projection neurons in lamina I, like those in cat, rat and monkey, show modality-selective tuning (Craig et al., 2001; Davidson et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2006).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from this study and comparison to cited literature.

claim: A subset of Bhlhe22-derived cells in the superficial dorsal horn are inhibitory neurons that function to inhibit itch.
source: Previous studies from our lab revealed that a subset of Bhlhe22-derived cells in the superficial dorsal horn are inhibitory neurons that function to inhibit itch (Ross et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work from the authors' lab.

claim: Bhlhe22-Cre neurons receive direct input from primary afferents that respond to capsaicin, mustard oil, and menthol.
source: We also showed previously, using slice recordings, that Bhlhe22-Cre neurons receive direct input from primary afferents that respond to capsaicin, mustard oil, and menthol, raising the possibility that some Bhlhe22-Cre neurons might mediate the inhibition of itch by counter-stimuli (Kardon et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Most Bhlhe22-Cre labeled neurons fired in response to at least one stimulus type (mechanical, cold, or heat).
source: We found that most Bhlhe22-Cre labeled neurons fired in response to at least one stimulus type, and that some responded to all three (Figure 4C) as summarized (Figure 4Ci; pie chart).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: Some Bhlhe22-Cre neurons responded to all three types of stimuli (mechanical, cold, and heat).
source: We found that most Bhlhe22-Cre labeled neurons fired in response to at least one stimulus type, and that some responded to all three (Figure 4C) as summarized (Figure 4Ci; pie chart).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: Bhlhe22-Cre neurons fire action potentials in response to three types of counter-stimuli: heat, cold and mechanical force.
source: Thus, whereas our previous slice recordings had revealed that Bhlhe22-Cre cells receive direct input from afferents that respond to counter-stimuli (Kardon et al., 2014), the ex vivo recordings presented here show, for the first time, that Bhlhe22-Cre neurons fire action potentials in response to three types of counter-stimuli, heat, cold and mechanical force.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from this study and comparison to previous work.

claim: Cutaneous stimulation evokes IPSCs in Bhlhe22-Cre neurons.
source: Interestingly, we observed that cutaneous stimulation evokes not only EPSCs (data not shown) but also IPSCs in Bhlhe22-Cre neurons (Figure 4D), suggesting that feed-forward inhibition may gate the responses of Bhlhe22-Cre neurons following stimulation of the skin.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: Feed-forward inhibition may gate the responses of Bhlhe22-Cre neurons following stimulation of the skin.
source: Interestingly, we observed that cutaneous stimulation evokes not only EPSCs (data not shown) but also IPSCs in Bhlhe22-Cre neurons (Figure 4D), suggesting that feed-forward inhibition may gate the responses of Bhlhe22-Cre neurons following stimulation of the skin.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observation of IPSCs.

claim: Brightly fluorescent cells can be targeted for recording as long as they are within 70 µm from the surface of the spinal cord.
source: Moreover, we could target these brightly fluorescent cells as long as they were within 70 µm from the surface of the spinal cord, suggesting it is possible to study interneurons that reside from lamina I through to the outer part of lamina III.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations during recordings.

claim: It is possible to study interneurons that reside from lamina I through to the outer part of lamina III using this preparation.
source: Moreover, we could target these brightly fluorescent cells as long as they were within 70 µm from the surface of the spinal cord, suggesting it is possible to study interneurons that reside from lamina I through to the outer part of lamina III.
evidence: This is inferred from the recording depth capability.

claim: Blue light induced strong inward currents in both Nts-Cre and Bhlhe22-Cre neurons expressing ChR2.
source: Whether recording from cells marked by the Nts-Cre allele or by the Bhlhe22-Cre allele, we found that blue light induced strong inward currents with amplitudes were not statistically different between populations (Figure 5A, B and D).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: The amplitudes of blue light-induced inward currents were not statistically different between Nts-Cre and Bhlhe22-Cre neurons.
source: Whether recording from cells marked by the Nts-Cre allele or by the Bhlhe22-Cre allele, we found that blue light induced strong inward currents with amplitudes were not statistically different between populations (Figure 5A, B and D).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: Blue light resulted in the generation of EPSCs in Nts-Cre neurons but not in Bhlhe22-Cre neurons.
source: However, it was only in Nts-Cre neurons, not Bhlhe22-Cre neurons, that blue light resulted in the generation of EPSCs (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: The evoked inward current in ChR2-expressing neurons was time-locked to the blue light.
source: Furthermore, while the evoked inward current was time-locked to the blue light, the EPSCs in Nts-Cre neurons persisted long after the termination of the stimulus.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations of the temporal relationship between stimulus and response.

claim: The EPSCs in Nts-Cre neurons persisted long after the termination of the blue light stimulus.
source: Furthermore, while the evoked inward current was time-locked to the blue light, the EPSCs in Nts-Cre neurons persisted long after the termination of the stimulus.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in the data.

claim: The cell autonomous effects of optogenetic activation were similar in Nts-Cre and Bhlhe22-Cre neurons, but the consequences to network activity in these two populations was distinct.
source: Thus, while the cell autonomous effects of optogenetic activation were similar in Nts-Cre and Bhlhe22-Cre neurons, the consequences to network activity in these two populations was distinct.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of direct effects versus network effects in the two populations.

claim: ChR2-expressing Nts-Cre neurons were able to follow a low frequency (0.1 Hz; 5 ms) optogenetic stimulation with one (and occasionally two) action potentials evoked with negligible latency jitter.
source: ChR2-expressing Nts-Cre neurons were able to follow a low frequency (0.1 Hz; 5 ms), where one (and occasionally two) action potentials were evoked with negligible latency jitter (Figure 5Ei and F).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: At higher frequencies (2 and 10 Hz), ChR2-expressing Nts-Cre neurons could not consistently follow optogenetic stimulation, demonstrating an increase in jitter and frequent failures.
source: In contrast, at higher frequencies (2 and 10 Hz), these neurons could not consistently follow, demonstrating an increase in jitter and frequent failures (Figure 5Eii, 5iii and 5F).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: ChR2-expressing Bhlhe22-Cre neurons showed worse fidelity to optogenetic stimulation than Nts-Cre neurons.
source: Moreover, when similar experiments were performed in ChR2-expressing Bhlhe22-Cre neurons, these cells showed even worse fidelity to optogenetic stimulation, and many showed a reluctance to fire even when we increased the stimulus duration (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F and G).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in the supplemental figure.

claim: When using the Ai32 allele, approximately three weeks' time post-recombination is required to reach functional levels of ChR2 expression in the dorsal horn.
source: Thus, when using the Ai32 allele, it appears that approximately three weeks' time post-recombination is required to reach functional levels of ChR2 expression in the dorsal horn.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data comparing different time points after tamoxifen injection.

claim: Expression of either Arch or Halo in dorsal horn neurons enabled light-induced outward current and hyperpolarization that was not significantly different between Nts-Cre and Bhlhe22-Cre populations.
source: Expression of either Arch or Halo in dorsal horn neurons enabled light-induced outward current (Figure 6A, B and C) and hyperpolarization (Figure 6D, E and F) that was not significantly different between Nts-Cre and Bhlhe22-Cre populations.
evidence: This is based on experimental data and statistical analysis shown in the figure.

claim: In Nts-Cre neurons expressing Arch, optogenetic stimulation almost completely blocked root-evoked action potentials.
source: In Nts-Cre neurons expressing Arch, optogenetic stimulation almost completely blocked root-evoked action potentials (Figure 6D and G).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: The number of root-evoked action potentials was significantly reduced by optogenetic inhibition of Bhlhe22-Cre neurons expressing Halo, but they were not completely eliminated.
source: In contrast, while the number of root-evoked action potentials was significantly reduced by optogenetic inhibition of Bhlhe22-Cre neurons expressing Halo, they were not completely eliminated (Figure 6E and G).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: The disparity in effectiveness between Arch and Halo is likely due, at least in part, to differences between the two types of recorded cells, potentially including distinct intrinsic properties and/or differences in root-evoked input.
source: Given the similarity in outward current and hyperpolarization elicited by the two inhibitory opsins, the disparity in their effectiveness is likely due, at least in part, to differences between the two types of recorded cells, potentially including distinct intrinsic properties and/or differences in root-evoked input.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the experimental observations.

claim: Bhlhe22-Cre neurons can inhibit lamina I neurons directly, clamping their activity and preventing them from firing.
source: These findings suggest that Bhlhe22-Cre neurons can inhibit this recorded cell directly, clamping its activity and preventing it from firing.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data showing that optogenetic activation of Bhlhe22-Cre neurons prevents action potentials in the recorded cell despite EPSCs.

claim: Of six projection neurons that were functionally characterized, only four received monosynaptic input from Nts-Cre neurons.
source: Of six projection neurons that were functionally characterized, only four received monosynaptic input from Nts-Cre neurons (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: There was no evidence that Nts-Cre neurons selectively target projection neurons that are tuned to a specific stimulus modality.
source: However, in this small set of characterized cells we found no evidence that Nts-Cre neurons selectively target projection neurons that are tuned to a specific stimulus modality, which may not be surprising given that Nts-Cre cells are likely a heterogeneous population.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from a small sample, with speculation about the reason.

claim: Most lamina I neurons have center-surround receptive fields.
source: We revealed that most lamina I neurons have center-surround receptive fields, and that some showed prolonged afterdischarge.
evidence: This is based on experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Some lamina I neurons showed prolonged afterdischarge.
source: We revealed that most lamina I neurons have center-surround receptive fields, and that some showed prolonged afterdischarge.
evidence: This is based on experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Inhibition is thought to be involved in limiting nociception, sharpening spatial acuity, and providing occlusion between somatosensory modalities.
source: Inhibition is thought to be involved in limiting nociception, sharpening spatial acuity, and providing occlusion between somatosensory modalities, all of which become disrupted upon injury (Lewin et al., 1994).
evidence: This is based on established scientific knowledge and cited literature.

claim: Inhibitory processes involved in limiting nociception, sharpening spatial acuity, and providing occlusion between somatosensory modalities become disrupted upon injury.
source: Inhibition is thought to be involved in limiting nociception, sharpening spatial acuity, and providing occlusion between somatosensory modalities, all of which become disrupted upon injury (Lewin et al., 1994).
evidence: This is based on cited literature.

claim: The number of different subtypes of spinal projection neurons is unknown.
source: In particular, the number of different subtypes of spinal projection neurons is unknown, and how they encode somatosensory information is unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: How spinal projection neurons encode somatosensory information is unclear.
source: In particular, the number of different subtypes of spinal projection neurons is unknown, and how they encode somatosensory information is unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Afterdischarge is observed in naïve rats upon recording from superficial dorsal horn neurons in vivo, where 20% of dorsal horn neurons showed prolonged responses to a single stimulus.
source: Moreover, afterdischarge is also observed in naïve rats upon recording from superficial dorsal horn neurons in vivo, where (just was we report here) 20% of dorsal horn neurons showed prolonged responses to a single stimulus (Woolf and Fitzgerald, 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The spared nerve injury model has been shown to cause mechanical hypersensitivity not only in the sural nerve territory but also in the saphenous nerve territory.
source: Furthermore, the spared nerve injury model has been shown to cause mechanical hypersensitivity not only in the sural nerve territory but also in the saphenous nerve territory (Decosterd and Woolf, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The ex vivo preparation remains compatible with several standard injury models for inflammatory and neuropathic pain.
source: Therefore, this ex vivo preparation remains compatible with several standard injury models for inflammatory and neuropathic pain.
evidence: This is inferred from the discussion of the saphenous nerve territory and injury models.

claim: Previously, double patch-clamp recordings have been used to investigate synaptic connectivity between interneuron subtypes, but this approach was limited by the fact that only 10% of the simultaneously recorded pairs of neurons were connected.
source: Previously, double patch-clamp recordings have been used to investigate synaptic connectivity between interneurons subtypes (Lu and Perl, 2005, 2003). But this approach was limited by the fact that only 10% of the simultaneously recorded pairs of neurons were connected.
evidence: This is based on cited literature describing previous approaches and their limitations.

claim: The combination of optogenetics and the ability to record from known cell types in the dorsal horn will allow rapid development of spinal wiring diagrams.
source: In contrast, the combination of optogenetics and the ability to record from known cell types in the dorsal horn will allow rapid development of spinal wiring diagrams.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential of the new approach.

claim: The typical criteria used to establish mono-synaptic connectivity using electrical stimulation (absence of failure upon stimulation at 20 Hz for Aδ fibers and 2 Hz for C fibers) is not applicable to optogenetic stimulation.
source: In particular, the typical criteria used to establish mono-synaptic connectivity using electrical simulation (absence of failure upon stimulation at 20 Hz for Aδ fibers and 2 Hz for C fibers [Nakatsuka et al., 1999]) is not applicable to optogenetic stimulation, since light-evoked action potentials have longer latency and show Cre latency jitter than those evoked by electric stimulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations and cited literature.

claim: Light-evoked action potentials have longer latency and show greater latency jitter than those evoked by electric stimulation.
source: In particular, the typical criteria used to establish mono-synaptic connectivity using electrical simulation (absence of failure upon stimulation at 20 Hz for Aδ fibers and 2 Hz for C fibers [Nakatsuka et al., 1999]) is not applicable to optogenetic stimulation, since light-evoked action potentials have longer latency and show Cre latency jitter than those evoked by electric stimulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in the supplemental figure.

claim: A less stringent criterion (e.g., 0.1 Hz optogenetic stimulation) was used to differentiate between mono- and polysynaptic input in the dorsal horn.
source: For this reason, we and others used a less stringent criterion (e.g., 0.1 Hz optogenetic stimulation) to differentiate between mono- and polysynaptic input in the dorsal horn (Honsek et al., 2015; Wang and Zylka, 2009; Cui et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on the authors' approach and cited literature.

claim: Verification of monosynaptic connections will likely require additional tests involving, for instance, the use of tetrodotoxin together with the potassium channel antagonist 4-aminopyridine.
source: Verification of monosynaptic connections will likely require additional tests involving, for instance, the use of tetrodotoxin together with the potassium channel antagonist 4-aminopyridine (Nelson et al., 2014; Petreanu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future experimental approaches, supported by citations.

claim: Spinal projection neurons represent only 5% of total neurons in lamina I.
source: However, while many spinal projection neurons are located in lamina I, they can be difficult to target since they are quite sparse, representing only 5% of total neurons in this lamina (Todd, 2010).
evidence: This is based on cited literature.

claim: The Nts-Cre allele labels approximately half of excitatory neurons in the superficial dorsal horn.
source: In initial experiments, we compared the Nts-Cre allele, which is specific to excitatory neurons, and labels approximately half of those in the superficial dorsal horn (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) to the Bhlhe22-Cre allele, which mainly labels inhibitory neurons, including those that express Nos1 (also known as nNOS) and/or Galanin (Chiang et al., 2016; Kardon et al., 2014; Ross et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in the supplemental figure.

claim: The Bhlhe22-Cre allele mainly labels inhibitory neurons, including those that express Nos1 and/or Galanin.
source: In initial experiments, we compared the Nts-Cre allele, which is specific to excitatory neurons, and labels approximately half of those in the superficial dorsal horn (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) to the Bhlhe22-Cre allele, which mainly labels inhibitory neurons, including those that express Nos1 (also known as nNOS) and/or Galanin (Chiang et al., 2016; Kardon et al., 2014; Ross et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on cited literature.

claim: The magnitude of blue light-evoked current in Nos1-CreER cells was significantly lower than that observed using either Nts-Cre or Bhlhe22-Cre alleles.
source: As before, blue light induced inward current in ChR2-expressing cells (Figure 5C); however, the magnitude of the current was significantly lower than that observed using either Nts-Cre or Bhlhe22-Cre alleles (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is based on experimental data and statistical analysis shown in the figure.

claim: The reduced current in Nos1-CreER cells was due to the timing of Cre-mediated recombination, which occurred only upon tamoxifen-treatment, hence allowing less time for ChR2 accumulation.
source: Given that Nos1 neurons make up a large fraction of those marked by the Bhlhe22-Cre allele, it seemed unlikely that this disparity in current was due to a difference in cell type. Rather, we hypothesized that the reduced current in Nos1-CreER cells was due to the timing of Cre-mediated recombination, which occurred only upon tamoxifen-treatment, hence allowing less time for ChR2 accumulation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on inference from the experimental observations.

claim: If the time post tamoxifen was reduced to one week rather than three, the amplitude of blue light-evoked current was smaller still, and insufficient to trigger an action potential in ChR2-expressing cells.
source: Consistent with this, we found that if we reduced the time post tamoxifen (i.e., one week rather than three), the amplitude of blue light-evoked current was smaller still, and insufficient to trigger an action potential in ChR2-expressing cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D and E).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in the supplemental figure.

claim: The effects of optogenetic stimulation in a given cell type must be determined empirically.
source: These data reveal that, while ChR2 can be used in our somatosensory preparation to manipulate the activity of genetically defined cells, the effects of optogenetic stimulation in a given cell type must be determined empirically.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations showing variable effects across cell types.

claim: The effects of inhibitory opsins are context-dependent.
source: Thus, these findings illustrate that inhibitory opsins can be used in a variety of cell types in the dorsal horn to manipulate cell activity while underscoring the important concept that their effects are context-dependent.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations showing different effectiveness in different contexts.
